items.body: Review by tszirmay — Przemyslaw Rudz and Roman Odoj have teamed together to offer electronic prog with a swift kick in the backside , a beefy release that has more muscles than Arnold Schwarzenegger, recalling more early Ultravox/John Foxx, what with the thrilling bass propulsion and the razor-sharp guitar work (from Odoj) and Rudz elaborating on the electronics side with some slicing synthesizer runs that defy the imagination. The homage paid to all the great electronic pioneers from the Berlin and Dusseldorf schools being the most obvious but equally involving many of the current breed of synthesists. The title track wastes zero time in getting the blood flowing, a fast and furious turbo-charge race on the highway. Arkadiusz Suchara on bass does a masterful job at thickening the sauce, while Michal Malinski pounds the living daylight out of his kit, channeling Warren Cann in the process. A brooding track that reflects perhaps the current turbulence in that area of the world, regularly prone to conflict of one kind or another. The limitless tonalities radiating from Rudz's synthesizer arsenal are tectonic, by the end of this opener, there is little doubt that the mind will be satisfied until the very end. And what an ending we have in store! The extended 'Pyramidion ' is overtly more orchestral, not too far removed from Mark Shreeve, in that it's a brawnier form of sequencing, a lusher class of melodic sweeps and a granite rhythmic foundation that pounds mightily. Laying some dense electric guitar layers only thickens the recipe, Odoj unafraid of soaring and scouring the horizon for new territories while Rudz locks in a series of overlapping synthesizers structures that, while keeping it relatively simple, combines expertly with a more forceful attitude that cannot be denied. Over thirteen minutes of unrelenting sounds, completely thrilling. Knowing full well the benefits of melancholy, a Polish specialty that comes across in glorified fashion on the dreamy 'Two Faces of Autumn, Rudz and Odoj propose a total transition into an altogether different style, where clanging guitar chords, pooling e-piano motifs, and substantial orchestral swaths of electronic strings luxuriate in ethereal splendor. The romanticism is overt, expressing the transformation of green into red and then brown, the hot sun replaced by driving rain, the winds warning of an eventual winter rolling in, unfettered. The effect-laden guitars flicker gently in the cool twilight, long enough for the magnanimous pipe organ to absolve all the sins of the summer and prepare for the seasonal atonement. 'Into the Higher Domain' is a substantial 20-minute sonic exorcism, a respectful invitation to introspection, in full accordance with the powers above, a very cathedral sounding symphony that wavers between Vangelis and Tangerine Dream. With its overtly arching properties there is a suggestion that the fight has now become flight, an extra corporal voyage with a synthesized sax patch and a wonderful acoustic guitar phrasing amid the reverberating e-piano puddles. Shifting into the upper cosmos, the sounds become more compressed, as if forged by the atmospheric pressures of escaping into the void. By the 10-minute mark, the stark reality kicks in with some rivet-busting commotions, issued from both key and fret boards, as if dueling with charged shrieks to achieve some kind of dominance. The guitar-synth work is a mixture of slippery Asian sounds (Yellow Magic Orchestra meets Bill Nelson) and dense industrial pounding, excitable synthesizer forays spinning in a myriad of directions, and depth-charge bass rumbles notwithstanding. Mesmerizing electro stuff. My version of the album comes with a bonus track, a stupendous instrumental cover of 'Watchers of the Skies', yes, you read correctly, the Genesis classic! Rudz and Odoj pay their respects by altering the technical elements without sacrificing the unalterable core beauty of the piece, the synthesizers starker than the original, the mellotron kept honorific. Bravo. 4.5 airport sendoffs.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由波兰音乐人 Przemysław Rudz 与 Roman Odoj 合作的前卫电子专辑，融合了柏林与杜塞尔多夫学派合成器传统的精髓，同时加入锐利的吉他层与强劲的贝斯推进。开篇曲以高速节奏与厚重音墙直击感官，延续了 John Foxx 时代 Ultravox 的冷峻张力；长达十三分钟的'Pyramidion'转向更管弦乐化的序列编排，厚重而有层次，吉他与合成器相互叠加形成壮阔声景。'Two Faces of Autumn'则展现了波兰式的忧郁气质，钢琴、电风琴与效果吉他交织出季节更替的沉思画面。终曲'Into the Higher Domain'是二十分钟的声学净化仪式，介于 Vangelis 与 Tangerine Dream 之间的大教堂式交响，暗示从战斗到逃离的内在转变。整张专辑在合成器音色探索、情绪层次与结构编排上都展现出高度成熟的匠心。

items.body: A Silence Opens is the third, and unfortunately, the last album of the Columbia Icefield, the quartet that trumpeter Nate Wooley founded, and featuring pedal steel master Susan Alcorn, guitarist-vocalist Ava Mandoza, and drummer Ryan Sawyer. A Silence Opens is informed by the death of close ones and the endless grief their death entails, and began as a tribute to the trumpeter Ron Miles (who passed away in March 2022), Wooley's mentor and someone he looked up to as an older brother, credited for saving Wooley’s life and making him a better person, expanded to a memorial album for Alcorn, whose idiosyncratic sound distinguished the quartet’s sound, who passed away in January 2025, while Columbia Icefield completed the album. Wooley writes: “Death is a lack with weight. At the moment that you realize that someone you love is irrecoverably gone, a small tear in your life opens up. As days go by, the sliver of grief grows, becoming a rift, a gap, a gulley, a canyon. At the point that you feel lost in the immensity of space where that person used to be, the expansion stops; the hole—the vast and airy part of your life that used to be occupied by that person—becomes solid. Maybe it decreases in size, but more likely, your memories grow to occupy its space”. Wooley decided to transform the “pressure with sadness” and fill the silence and the vacuum that death brings with new sounds and new voices, creating a deeply emotional and life-affirming musical statement. The album includes three Miles’ pieces, and Alcorn’s favorite protest song - Chilean singer-songwriter Víctor Jara’s “El Derecho De Vivir En Paz” (The Right to Live in Peace, the song that closes Alcorn’s Canto album, Relative Pitch, 2023). The third, unrehearsed interpretation of this song featured a choir of Alcorn’s friends - Mary Halvorson, Ingrid Laubrock, Wendy Eisenberg, gabby fluke-mogul, Laura Ortman, Patrick Holmes, with Wooley, Mandoza, and Sawyer. “We just felt the joy—in saying thank you, we love you, and goodbye—that Susan would have taken in seeing friends and bandmates all lined up, eyes closed, following the lines of a melody she felt in her heart”, Wooley says. A Silence Opens immediately occupies your full attention with its powerful emotional urgency, faithfully capturing the complex musical essence and personas of Miles and Alcorn. It is structured as a mournful suite or ritual that celebrates the lives and the gift of knowing Miles and Alcorn. It begins with Wooley’s vulnerable whistling solo, the melody of “El Derecho De Vivir En Paz”, followed by Miles’ ballad “Howard Beach” (from My Cruel Heart, Gramavision, 1996), with Mendoza contrasting and pushing Wooley’s touching and soulful playing into aggressive storms; then Mendoza, who almost cries as she recites “El Derecho”; Miles’ dramatic “Darken My Door” (from I Am a Man , Yellowbird, 2017); the choir who “El Derecho” in a waythat makes you want to join their singing; Wooley’s poetic centerpiece, “We Say Goodbye Twice/Wildwood Flower”, that distills the musical and emotional core of this inspiring, heartfelt album with Alcorn’s arresting playing; the quartet offering a joyful interpertation of “El Derecho””; an intense and urgent, distortion-heavy and propulsive version of Miles “You Taste” (from Woman’s Day , Gramavision, 1997); and concluding with Wooley’s solo trumpet of “El Derecho”, simultaneously singing and crying this song, and then whistles it, marking a final acceptance of the passed one, and also as a requiem for Columbia Icefield itself, until it disappears in silence. Columbia Icefield was in many ways a kind of musical family, and it sounds like a close-knit musical organism. It was one of those few, rare bands that keep expanding its musical universe with every new album, a band that you cherish all its albums, a band that is larger than its parts. “May we always bear the weight of these losses as a gift of presence and memory,” Wooley concluded. items._cn_summary: 这是Columbia Icefield乐队的第三张也是最后一张专辑，由小号手Nate Wooley创立，成员包括踏板钢吉他大师Susan Alcorn、吉他手兼主唱Ava Mendoza及鼓手Ryan Sawyer。专辑源于对两位已故音乐人的悼念——Wooley的导师小号手Ron Miles于2022年去世，而Alcorn在专辑制作期间于2025年辞世。整张作品以仪式化的挽歌结构展开，Wooley以脆弱的口哨独奏引入智利歌手Víctor Jara的反战歌曲《El Derecho De Vivir En Paz》，随后融入Miles的原创曲目。专辑末尾Alcorn的友人组成合唱团即兴演唱该曲，呈现出原始的集体哀悼氛围。乐队将悲痛转化为声音的探索，融合自由即兴、踏板钢吉他音色实验与社会抗议歌曲文本，形成兼具私密情感与公共纪念性质的终曲。

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, with a title like that, I just could not resist: Rodrigo Maccioni is certainly no fool and I am far from either blind, or deaf for that matter! Alejandro Vera handles the bassoon, Pascal Montenegro on English horn, Alfonso Vergara plays clarinets, Arianne Guerra the viola with bassist Eduardo Rubio and drummer Leonardo Saavedra, adding Jorge Bugue�o on electric piano and ably led by Rodrigo Maccioni on electric guitar, keyboards and flute. Now, to be fair, RIO/Avant is not necessarily within my expertise but If I am to be called a Prog Rogue, I must live up to being open-minded and occasionally swim against any tide. Also, I quite enjoyed Penguin Caf� Orchestra, so I should be okay. Vamos! The title track opens the curtains with courageous flair, a gigantic nearly 22-minute epic that takes boldness to new heights, an orchestral effect where all the musicians get to blend in and interface with precision. Overflowing with twists and turns and the occasional somersault, I was particularly captivated by the stunning viola and clarinet elements, as well as the muscular drum work and when the bassoon and horns kicked in, the amazement was palpable. Rodrigo certainly has a keen ability to marshal all the components into a cohesive centralized core, his mathematical electric guitar work showing not only rhythmic complexity, but the soloing can often bewilder with gushing emotional outcry. The arrangements are definitely intricately woven, the variations suggesting a hypnotic quality that cannot be ignored, and yet the entire opus is highly melodic and agreeable to the ear, with hints of dissonance and even playfulness that add the obligatory spice. Vergara's clarinet is often the highlight, as the warm sound of the instrument exudes a sense of fun that collides softly with all the surrounding mayhem. As far as experimental Prog is concerned, this piece is quite the mind-opener. The next three tracks are all under 8 minutes long and serve as sonic portals that seek to express various images that could have qualified as a suite, the reflective "Temple of Mirrors" aiming at more ambient scenarios, closer to modern classical soundtrack music. Here the strings are oblique, the percussion choosing percolation as well as propulsion, the bass boisterous and Rodrigo ripping hard on the fretboard. More of an experimental KC feel, Leonardo Saavedra channeling both his Muir and Bruford influences to perfection, a stunning slice of bravado. "When They Arrive" injects some mystery into the proceedings, the stark echoes of a science fiction scene apparent to these ears, somewhere between eerie and intriguing, the cacophony linear and purposeful, as the piano plays the conductor all along. The trilling sounds midway into the piece owe a sense of vibrating lizard tongues , amid the rhythmic aspic, a frightfully vivid touch that hit the mark. "Everything Stopped" explodes from the gates with furious abandon, shards of razor wire cutting into the skin and the mood bends into adrenalin-fueled numbness. The piano and English horn bounce off each other like two coy lovers, a synth painting the backdrop, the woodwinds curling delicately among the drumbeats, eventually led by the gripping viola into another sombre realm. Rodrigo takes over with a cyclical guitar pattern that settles the score into a more athletic environment. The insistence is punctuated by the bass /drum duo that shows little remorse in dragging the remaining instruments into the cauldron. A sustained final track ,"Memento Mori" summarizes the overall mood quite succinctly, a form of controlled bedlam that never seems to jar negatively, yet keeping the listener perpetually close to the edge, as if on a highwire. Peaks, valleys, entrances and exits are all undertaken to bring the listener to some distant space, a comfortable confusion that can never be predetermined. Kudos to all the musicians who weld together with apparent impunity, led by Rodrigo who never hogs the limelight, content to orchestrate the various engaging sounds and shaping them into a cohesive whole. This was quite the personal experience, especially for a fan of melody who generally shies away from dissonance and turmoil. It certainly helped with my blood circulation and overall cardiovascular disposition. A band I intend to follow. 4.5 Aconcaguas
items._cn_summary: 智利音乐人Rodrigo Maccioni领衔的乐队以丰富古典乐器配置——巴松管、英国管、单簧管、中提琴——与电吉他、键盘、打击乐形成对话，编制罕见。首曲近22分钟的史诗级作品将管弦乐效果与前卫摇滚的数学性结构融为一体，节奏复杂、变奏密集，却保持高度旋律性。后续三首短曲分别探索环境氛围、科幻意象与爆发性张力，接近现代古典配乐质感。鼓手展现出Muir与Bruford双重影响，键盘担当指挥角色，电吉他独奏兼具技术密度与情感爆发。整体编曲精密，融合即兴、催眠式循环与微妙不和谐，呈现一幅跨越古典、爵士与前卫摇滚的实验画卷。

items.body: Photo by Nino Halm By Ljubisa Tosic* Anyone lucky enough to have seen Christian Lillinger's project Open Form for Society live in 2019 at Donaueschingen or at the Jazzfest Berlin will easily understand why he calls it a "sound organ." After years on hiatus, the drummer is now reviving this deeply resonant project. When one confronts Christian Lillinger with prominent colleagues' names, intending to find out how lasting his encounters with figures such as Rolf Kühn, Joachim Kühn, David Liebman, Alexander von Schlippenbach, or John Tchicai may have been, he responds with a staccato stream of additional names that have inscribed themselves into his musical biography: Tamara Stefanovich, Mat Maneri, Craig Taborn, Joe Lovano, Christopher Dell, Peter Brötzmann, Beat Furrer, Peter Evans, Sofia Jernberg, John Schröder, Bob Degen, Lotte Anker, Barre Phillips, Evan Parker, Wadada Leo Smith, William Parker, Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky, and many others... Of course. When it comes to lasting influence, says Lillinger, "It's a difficult matter." To speak only about 0.1 percent of those influences would be unfair. On the other hand, there were naturally his own decisions and major life steps that were connected to certain individuals. Lillinger speaks first of the decision "to start playing drums at all," and then of "having the opportunity, at sixteen, coming from a village, to study and pursue a professional path." Here the support of Günther "Baby" Sommer, a towering figure of free jazz, was essential. "Another decisive moment was getting to know Joachim Kühn, who encouraged me to manifest my own music." From this ultimately emerged Christian Lillinger's Grund, an ensemble known for its distinctive dynamic forms of interplay. If we continue digging deeper, Lillinger agrees that his search for a controlled freedom and openness in music-making is connected to personally perceived limitations- such as the traditional role of the drummer in jazz- as well as to his own biographical experiences: My outlook was shaped by independence from a very early age. At the same time, I believe the classical role of the jazz drummer should be one of further development and expansion. Tradition is a constantly evolving form while preserving its roots. For him, tradition also means, "being able to articulate oneself freely on one's instrument and develop one's own language." No surprise, then, that Lillinger regards jazz itself "as an art music" that demands alertness and continuous development. Only in this way, he argues, can one do justice to the legacy of great innovators and carry their heritage forward through one's own artistic stance. "Everything else is dead music to me- music that merely fulfills a certain mood or expectation and thereby loses its timelessness. That interests me very little..." Listening to Lillinger's music, it quickly becomes apparent that here is someone who hovers powerfully above stylistic boundaries. It is therefore tempting to throw a few more names and concepts at him to discover if he is influenced by contemporary classical music. Perhaps the aleatoric methods of John Cage or the open-form concepts of Karlheinz Stockhausen and Earle Brown play a role. Open Form for Society group shot. Photo by Nadja Hoehfeld. Perhaps the great sonic precision known from works by Pierre Boulez is also essential, particularly for the current and second recording by his ensemble Open Form For Society (OFFS). "Aleatoricism plays no role whatsoever in OFFS," says Lillinger. "My music is very concretely composed and written down in conventional notation." Nevertheless, influences from contemporary classical music are numerous. He describes them with terms such as "serial" and "microtonal." His musical thinking also revolves around traditions such as spectralism, New Complexity, and concepts of micro-time and irrational time. These are, he says, "important procedural and inspirational sources." Someone who formulates his ideas so consciously can perhaps summarize his aesthetic position in something approaching a manifesto: It is a "new new" chamber music that incorporates space into its actions just as much as what is prescribed and written. The placement and interpretation of the notes are always in dialogue with spatiality. The performers create the space; within this space they navigate themselves. I am opposed to genre labels, so I would rather speak of "post-genre" and of "composer-performers," because everyone involved bears responsibility for shaping and further developing the material. It is a music that operates in a certain scientific manner and thereby continuously discovers new paths. Immersing oneself in the recording Open Form for Society II (Plaist), one feels as though embarking on a journey through an enchanted sonic garden that gathers collective musical reflexes and conveys an atmosphere of highly energized, controlled freedom. At times there are slowed-down events reminiscent of musical stalactite caves, as in "Aufgefächert." Elsewhere pulsating sound structures emerge, creating an almost nervous sonic world. Abstract piano figures and energetically charged sound spaces continually return, while density is omnipresent within this sounding architecture. "Vector" and "Ocker" recall an originally abstracted and further-developed bebop aesthetic, yet with their own freely treated thematic material and repetitive patterns. Introspective and expressive structures form the poles of this musical universe. How does such a world, constantly shifting between these poles, come into being? Does the personnel come first, or the composition? It is a very heterogeneous process, one that I wanted to pursue as naturally as possible. Initially there was the vision of assembling a larger ensemble with a strongly percussive sonic language that reflects my way of seeing and realizing structure. Here the sound of Boulez's Sur Incises was an important inspiration. At the same time, his work with nearly all of the musicians involved in various ensembles was another important factor. Whether Dell Lillinger Westergaard [DLW], Stemeseder-Lillinger, the collaborations with Petter Eldh and Kaja Draksler, with Robert Landfermann, or with Anna D'Errico through my work with Klangforum Wien- all of this was formative and gave me a clear idea of how and what I can write and hear. It is fitting that Lillinger mentions Boulez's Sur Incises. With its instrumentation of three pianos, three harps, and three percussionists, it is a sonic laboratory, an organized form of energy that Lillinger has expanded upon. Alongside himself on drums and electronics are Kaja Draksler (upright piano), Elias Stemeseder (spinet and synthesizer), Georg Vogel (electric clavinet), Anna D'Errico and Cory Smythe (piano), bassists Robert Landfermann, Jonas Westergaard, and Petter Eldh, and Christopher Dell on vibraphone. The process of selecting collaborators was equally heterogeneous: The criteria emerged from previous work with all participants in different projects. For me, this ensemble is the perfect way to connect and transcend the worlds of classical music and modernity. Some musicians are primarily responsible for the text, others for further developments regarding sound. My musical utopia requires excellent preparation: precise reading, abstraction, further writing, and transcendence. In this ensemble I consciously distribute that responsibility. Transcendence, he says, is less a concept than "a result of working with the material itself. We combine influences from contemporary classical music, the avant-garde, and modern beat culture, creating a common point of fusion. Everyone involved must be capable of developing their own further plan based on what is written." What may sound free is nevertheless clearly prescribed in many respects and directions, including highly detailed polyphonic notation and rhythmic structures: [This project] has very little to do with conventional notions of freedom and openness. Freedom begins with the possibilities of variation and dynamics. Through repetition and the slow variation within those repetitions, an individual space emerges. Everything conditions everything else and appears as a shared whole: a meta-instrument, a sonic organism. Working with the same colleagues over a long period can, of course, lead to a comfortable routine. One knows what the other person will do, adapts accordingly, and clichés may emerge. Lillinger sees it differently. "I don't see that danger. Because I work with the same musicians over a long period, a genuine awareness develops of what the next stages might be." Intensive work and insight make it possible "to take those next steps. With consistent and continuous work, neither boredom nor routine arise." A convincing explanation. This leaves the title Open Form for Society , which seems to suggest a close connection between music and social thought. "The collective negotiation of the music I initiate serves as the foundation and basis for negotiation." Does this also concern ideas of an open, liberal society, or democracy? The latter, absolutely! It concerns the utopia of a continually improving social process sustained through negotiation and the collective discovery of solutions. However, I must say that this project is more a sound that accompanies and encourages open processes than one that fully embodies them. Because I am the composer and initiator, it ultimately belongs more to a closed, albeit flexible, structure. For the openness of jazz, it is far too fixed and strict; for classical music, however, it remains too open. "It therefore exists between these often rigid and ultimately inadequate categories and hopefully inspires further thinking about these social limitations. The point is this: Never stop communicating and working. Never stop thinking!" This is Lillinger's ambitious approach. One that could also help people outside music avoid more than a few traps of cliché and convention. *Interview originally published in Jazz Podium, translated from German. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 本文是对德国鼓手Christian Lillinger的专访，聚焦其「Open Form for Society」项目。该项目被他称为「声音器官」，在2019年Donaueschingen音乐节和柏林爵士节演出后曾暂停，现已重启。Lillinger师从自由爵士先驱Günther「Baby」Sommer，又受Joachim Kühn启发创立Grund乐团，奠定了追求「受控的自由与开放」的创作哲学。他罗列出与Rolf Kühn、David Liebman、Peter Brötzmann、Evan Parker、Wadada Leo Smith等大量前辈及同代音乐家的合作经历，展现其跨越风格边界的网络。Lillinger视爵士为一种「艺术音乐」，强调传统必须持续演化，认为仅满足氛围与期待的演奏是「死去的音乐」。他强调鼓手在爵士传统中的角色应不断扩展与深化，其音乐实践正是这一理念的体现。

items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz联合意大利前卫作曲家Paladino与诗人Ferrari，发行专辑《Songs of Compassion》，以十首作品延续其实验音乐血脉。音乐层面以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管与合成器织体，采用非线性和无调性手法，打破西方和声运动的听觉惯性，风格更接近Steve Reich与Philip Glass的简约主义脉络。人声部分以世界疲惫却充满权威的嗓音承载诗歌化的当代歌词，旋律如意识流般起伏，不拘泥于传统进行。歌词直面威权主义、法西斯抬头与对死亡的冥想，延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统却更具哲学深度。专辑由意大利小厂牌Silentes发行，整体呈现出跨界实验与政治表达的高度统一。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑延续了首作的风格，以自制乐器为核心特色——他们用废旧物品和杂物亲手打造了包括 tassofon、tubophone、kitchenofon 等一系列音色独特的乐器，在现代录音技术下呈现出令人惊讶的准确音高与丰富音质。作品融合了克莱兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、中东风等多种世界音乐元素，每首曲目都精心搭配乐器与风格：在克莱兹默曲中用自制单簧管搭配巴松管与急促打击乐，昆比亚风曲目中西班牙合唱与拉丁打击乐交相辉映，标题曲以非洲节拍木鱼、沙锤和摇铃构建层次，辅以马林巴琴的旋律线条与爵士化即兴。乐评特别指出乐队展现了出色的器乐演奏水准与即兴能力，整张专辑在趣味性与音乐性之间取得了平衡，同时传达了音乐本质超越乐器形态的核心理念——音乐人总能找到方式表达对节奏与旋律的热爱。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威Camilla Hole Trio在延续前作科幻合成器与传统民间素材融合探索之后的回归之作，但这次将重心转向更为扎根传统的方向。核心乐器是高音萨克斯，配合贝斯、鼓、模块化合成器和颤音琴的层叠色彩。乐评以开篇曲目《Springleik》为例，详解了他们的演奏方法：先由萨克斯呈示旋律，节奏组辅以支持，随后Kalman以贝斯接过旋律线并与萨克斯齐奏，Nesheim在节奏上进一步拓展空间，整首曲目逐渐转向自由即兴，萨克斯在收束时再次回溯主题。值得注意的是，三位成员在乐队中的角色并非固定不变，而是不断流动重组，这种打破常规分工的演奏方式是乐队的标志性特征。整张专辑延续了将挪威西部民间旋律与爵士即兴语言相结合的艺术路径。

items.body: The Visit by cris derksen The Visit isn�t an album built on compromises. The fourth release from Derksen, a Canadian from the North TallCree Reserve on her father�s side, and with a Mennonite lineage from her mother, pushes and cajoles her visions, where it�s the opening, full-throated improvisation of �White Gladis 1� (with singer Jennifer Kreisberg) or the encompassing haunting mood that grows up around �Lyre Birds.� She�s primarily a cellist, one who works across genres; one of the great joys here is it�s impossible to attach any kind of handle to the music. Just as you think you have it nailed down, the next track is something different, as with the the cello and programming of �aabaakwad� which becomes the wordless singing of �New Heya.� The Visit by cris derksen There�s a raw, unfettered beauty to the album, music made with passion and no restraints. There are a couple of songs here, but nothing that conforms to expectations, altering gears and direction, as when the strings and brass that arrive from nowhere to take over �Buffalo Girls.� The Visit by cris derksen But the emotional centrepiece here is �Lyre Birds,� with Derksen�s cello weaving sparely around the shards of spoken words, leading into the fluttering piano arpeggios of �Nice And Clean.� This is an album of surprises, leading down strange lanes and around brilliant corners that offer startling new views. As both composer and musician, Cris Derksen is more than a singular talent; she�s a person with a vision for her music, and she keeps true to it here. The Visit is not an easy listen, but it is eminently satisfying. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由加拿大原住民与门诺派混血大提琴手Cris Derksen创作，跨越多种风格边界，难以归类。专辑以充满即兴精神的开篇作品奠定基调，大提琴与电子编程交织，随后转入人声吟唱。弦乐与铜管的突然介入打破常规预期，而抒情诗般的口语碎片在大提琴稀疏的环绕下构成专辑的情感核心。大提琴作为主奏乐器贯穿始终，与钢琴琶音、电子编程、人声即兴等多种元素对话。作品充满原始而自由的美感，创作者坚持个人音乐愿景，不迎合既有框架。这张专辑不追求轻松聆听体验，却在结构与情绪转换中提供持续的满足感，展现出鲜明的独立艺术视角与文化融合深度。

items.body: “The minimal revolution is coming!” Stanze Fredde Records, an independent Italian label founded in Turin and active since 2024, has released the third edition of its annual compilation. Issued June 19, Stanze Fredde Vol. 3 is available now on vinyl, CD, and digital formats. The label was born, in its own words, “in the thermal shock of Turin.” Stanze Fredde moves through the harsh temperature shifts of the international minimal synth scene: the body in the club and the body alone at home, the cheap machine and the private wound, the young artist with no budget and too much feeling to leave dormant. Its stated mission is simple enough to sound almost severe: bring minimal, synth-driven music to a desolate cultural landscape, gather those cold young voices who translate emotion into synthesizers, and make space for work built from limited means rather than market logic. Rather than treating minimal synth and synthpunk as museum material, Stanze Fredde looks backward with bright eyes and a clenched sense of purpose, pulling old forms through the machinery of the present. Throughout the compilation, artists from across the current international underground occupy a shared room of brittle basslines, stark rhythms, and private signals, all of them drawn to music that can feel severe on the surface while carrying a strange emotional heat beneath. There is also a political texture to the label’s philosophy, even when no slogan is being raised. Stanze Fredde places growth over profit, curiosity over polish, and communal instinct over industry ladder-climbing. In a scene often reduced to fetish objects and genre shorthand, the label treats cold music as a living language: direct, wounded, mechanical, funny, austere, erotic, and occasionally cruel in the way a good synth line can be cruel when it knows exactly where to press. The third edition of the compilation continues that yearly project with another international survey of minimal synth, synthpunk, and related electronic mutations. It is a dispatch from a label still learning by doing, building with what is available, and trusting that small rooms, small runs, and small machines can still carry large emotional voltage. The roster gives that philosophy a geography. Bogotá’s Climas Interiores opens the set with “Ventanas”; the project’s own shorthand—drum machines, synthesizers, sequencers, and the urge to shout—could double as a miniature manifesto for the compilation. New York duo Intolerable Life, formed by Jean Lorenzo (Silent Em) and Melanie Giselle and carrying Uruguayan and Dominican roots, follows with “Today’s Specials,” bringing punk and jazz instincts into minimal synthpop. Mexico City’s Neue Strassen turns its engagement with post-punk, new wave, and Neue Deutsche Welle toward “Nostalgia del Futuro,” while Berlin’s Oberst Panizza, a founding member and co-composer of UFO Shadow and Velvet Condom, supplies “Novembre” from the robotic lineage of early electronic pop. That international traffic continues through Douce Angoisse, whose route from France through London, Montréal, and Buenos Aires has fed a provocative strain of electro-cabaret, and Bucharest’s Andrei Rublev, self-described as goth techno from Transylvania drenched in unorthodox melancholy. NAAKKA’s “Antifasisti” makes the politics explicit: the Tampere project identifies as anti-fascist, non-binary EBM, darkwave, and synthpunk, built from secondhand hardware rather than pristine technological abundance. Der Bürokrat’s “Crepa” brings together Jules and Ben—the respective forces behind Zug and Hammershøi—in a stripped Italian-French electro-minimal collision, while Vision Nebulosa follows with “Despojo,” extending the compilation’s Spanish-titled thread. The compilation’s German-Dutch machinery is equally deep. DerPolier, active since 2025, joins minimalist electronics to direct German-language writing on “Ausbildung ’89.” Utrecht’s Staatseinde, operating since 2006, brings its unruly meeting point of wave, EBM, NDW, and punk to “Cold Room,” while Amsterdam producer Willem Stinissen’s Raderkraft answers with “Das zimmer ist zu klein,” drawing on vintage machines and the freedom hidden inside their limitations. AvonRim’s “Too Much” and Stuttgart veteran Der Mussikant’s “Repulsina” extend that stubborn electronic lineage; the latter’s one-man project reaches back to 1980, when minimal electronics were still a rupture rather than a revival. Mørna’s “Titivisma tou Tipota” and Eye Desire’s “Techniques Warsaw” then pull the compilation’s linguistic map outward once again. Near the close, Manchester’s Chrysalid Homo offers “Prison Phone” from a group that calls its work post-nuclear electronic music, assembling synthesizers, sequencers, drum machines, voices, and spoken word in the city’s industrial heartlands. Fukuoka’s Mojo Beatnik follows with “Furthest Reaches,” self-styled “primitive mutant wave” animated by a devotion to vintage Korg machines. At-risk’s “Faulty Units” leads into Mexican project Fiesta de Disfraces and “Club Pesadilla,” a fitting final title for a compilation that repeatedly treats the club as refuge, laboratory, and nightmare. Taken together, these twenty tracks do not argue for one fixed definition of minimal music. They show how far a few machines, a voice, and an obstinate idea can travel. Stanze Fredde Vol. 3 is out now on vinyl, CD, and digital formats. Listen to the album below, and order it here. Stanze Fredde Vol. 3 by Stanze Fredde Records Follow Stanze Fredde: YouTube Instagram Facebook The post “The Minimal Revolution is Coming!” — Stanze Fredde Releases International Synth Compilation Vol. 3 appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items._cn_summary: 意大利都灵独立厂牌 Stanze Fredde 发行了年度合辑第三辑，收录来自波哥大、纽约、墨西哥城、柏林等地的国际地下电子音乐人作品。合辑聚焦极简合成器与合成器朋克场景，以脆裂贝斯线、硬朗节奏和私密信号为共同语汇。厂牌哲学强调成长优先于利润、好奇优于打磨，意图在贫瘠的文化景观中为以有限资源构建的情感驱动的电子音乐保留空间。参演艺术家涵盖鼓机、合成器、序列器驱动的冷峻作品，部分融合朋克与爵士直觉。整体延续了将极简合成器视为活语言而非博物馆藏品的立场——直接、受伤、机械、时而残酷，是一份来自仍在实践中学习的小厂牌的情感电压记录。

items._cn_summary: Archie Shepp于1969年在巴黎录制的这张专辑是自由爵士与先锋爵士交织的作品，标题曲长达20分钟，汇集了Roscoe Mitchell、Clifford Thornton、Lester Bowie、Sunny Murray等一批Art Ensemble of Chicago与Creative Construction Company的核心乐手。标题曲中Shepp以人声介入，搭配Laurence Devereaux演奏的西非巴拉风（Balafon），将非洲传统音色带入爵士语境。Dave Burrell的钢琴与Philly Joe Jones的鼓点为整张专辑提供了张力极强的节奏支撑。BYG Actuel系列作为法国独立厂牌，在1969至1971年间系统地记录了欧洲的自由爵士场景，这张专辑正是该系列中跨文化对话的重要一环，融合了非裔美国人音乐传统与非洲乐器语汇。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Inspired by the amazing chemistry between of singers Anastasya Korol and Latifah Smith, San Diego's metal-grounded eclecticians have found a new direction: blending intricate multi-voiced vocal weaves over and within the boys' jazzified metal music.1. "Prelude" (1:32) an a cappella shanty performed as a layered four-part choral piece by Anastasya Korol and Latifah Smith. It definitely introduces the new approach the band is choosing for the album as well as sets the tone for the essential if not primary role that sophisticatedly-arranged vocals will have over the course of each of the next eight songs. (4.5/5) 2. "Pirates" (4:59) an amazingly fresh weave of near-liturgical choral vocal music with/within sophisticated heavy, metal, and Jazz-Rock Fusion music. The shocking first minute blows away, the vocal arrangements of the second impressing big time, while the jazzy instrumental third-through-fifth sucks you into its groove and keyboard magic while the finale reminds you that these sacred songs are sea shanties. A lot like INNER EAR BRIGADE! (9.25/10)3. "Gambler" (2:57) a very INNER EAR BRIGADE and iNFiNiEN-sounding tune with Anastasya and Latifah blending their voices over the funky prog music, sounding like something from SAY SHE SHE as well as the afore-mentioned quirk masters. Amazing! (9.5/10)4. "Ice Eater" (4:21) more incredibly refreshing sophisticated choral vocal weaving woven seamlessly within some awesome heavy jazzy prog. The vocal arrangements are so pert and professional, reminding me of so many of today's incredibly inventive female-led bands like A FORMAL HORSE, iNFiNiEN, INNER EAR BRIGADE, THE MOULETTES, PLANTOID, BILLIE BOTTLE'S TEMPLE OF SHIBBOLETH, RESONAXIS, and even HANDS OF THE HERON and LYNSEY WARD's projects. (9.333/10)5. "Archons" (2:33) the cheeky vocal performance here reminds me of both Aussie band RESONAXIS as well as KATHARINE BLAKE's projects and Billie Bottle's Temple of Shibboleth. Great theatric piano-based music beneath the vocal choir makes it all possible. Probably the most beautiful song on the album. Awesome! (9.667/10)6. "Desert" (4:23) Latin-infused heavy Jazz-Rock Fusion with a theatric weave of cabaret-like vocals intertwined within results in another tune that has a cheek and frivolity to it--until 1:37 when Matthew, Ryan, Nathan, and Kevin open a door to horror soundtrack music while Anastasya and Latifah provide the light wordless vocalese "ooh"s. Then the song moves through a few other syncopated motifs over which the vocal choir performs as if in ceremonial or theatric setting. Interesting and respectable but ultimately a little too jagged edged for me to maintain my engagement and/or enjoyment. (8.75/10)7. "Thing Eater" (5:48) another song based on even more dominating angular melody lines: presenting what feels like rock music that is much more constructed and composed around modern chromatic Classical Music traditions ("atonality," "Serialism," or "Expressionism"?). It's impressive but never as accessible or engaging as the album's other material. (8.75/10)8. "Elegy" (6:54) male voices in the choir! This piano-based piece feels as if it truly needs a house of worship for its presentation. During the first half of this I find myself reminded of 2000s Texas phenomenon POLYPHONIC SPREE while at others I find myself thinking of some of the great Broadway musicals I've heard (especially Stephen Schwartz' Godspell). Even the infrequent injections of aggressive angular electric guitar do little to detract from the celestial/liturgical or courtly feel of this wonderful piece of music. I think Katharine Blake (Medi�val B�bes), Hannah Moule (The Moulettes), Lynsey Ward and her Espera trio, and Bristol, England's Hands Of The Heron would be proud and envious of the achievement made here. (9.5/10)9. "Recapitulation" (1:16) a folk-feeling four-voiced a cappella vocal finale--much like the album's opener--to wind things up. A perfect ending to an incredible album. (4.375/5) Total Time 35:12I am so grateful for the drastically improved sound engineering and album length (the two criticisms I've posted for all of the band's previous three albums). I really love the way the band's vocalists have gelled--how they've become confident enough in the choral approach to their vocal deliveries. I don't know if Anastasya and Latifah are doing all of the choral tracks themselves (I don't hear male voices in some of the songs) but it's okay (brilliant!): whatever they're doing/however they're doing it, it's amazing! And mega-kudos to the guys for going along with, supporting, even whole-heartedly embracing it!A-/five stars; an amazing and totally refreshing album of progressive rock music, putting on display, once again, the fact that the new artists of the 21st Century have got all of the tools and brains to keep pushing the boundaries of possibility for our beloved genre of music.
items._genre: avant-prog / jazz-rock fusion / choral art rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自圣地亚哥乐队，以复杂的合唱编排与爵士化金属融合为核心方向。两位主唱Anastasya Korol与Latifah Smith在器乐骨架上铺设多声部人声织体，从开篇的无伴奏合唱预叙到海妖主题的礼仪化声乐与重金属交织，呈现出类似当代女性主导前卫乐队的精致手法。作品中融合了自由爵士、拉丁元素、卡巴莱式戏剧化演唱以及序列主义无调性手法，结构上虽偏向拼贴式段落组合，但部分曲目在风格转换上稍显生硬。整体呈现学院派编曲思维与人声实验的结合，是一张在声乐编排层面具有较强辨识度的作品。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — This Russian band's 17th studio album release! Can you believe they've been pumping them out since 2005! And, despite retaining a consistent core of musicians, they keep evolving.1. "Cendo" (5:54) electrified and effected acoustic guitar, fretless bass, gritty synth washes, and waves of cymbal sounds open this before the band launch into a jazz-rockin' motif that is rooted in traditional folk forms and melodies (amplified when Alexander Koryukovets' accordion joins in). The two concurrent lead guitar lines are the song's most distinguishing feature (aside from the accordion and Russian folk feel). Overall, I like it though it feels, compositionally, a little loose and unpolished to me (and the fact that Ivan Fedotov's drumming during song's second half feels out of sync with the rest of the band). At times it's just a bit too messy and cacophonous. (8.75/10)2. "Issero" (6:21) a very satisfying multi-motif song that starts out very warm and comforting--sounding like a blend of something from Robin Guthrie's chord bank and Paul Speer's atmospheric guitar world before Arkady Fedotov's antelope-like fretless bass enters with Alexander Kuzovlev's Steve Vai/Jeff Beck-like "floating" volume-pedal-manipulated lead electric guitar note play taking up the lead position. While at first I like Arkady's work very much, when he settles in the lowest registers of his sound capacity it muddies the song terribly--detracting from the rest of the weave. From there there are three other motifs, a brief bridge of synth-generated Ozrics/Kosmisches swirly sounds, a heavy fast-moving rocker over which Alex Kuz plays "mandoline" while rhythm guitarist Vladimir Ryabinin chugs along on some deep near-metal chords and then a final return (via folk instrument bridge) to Jazz-lite world music with gentle power chord strums of Vlad's electrified acoustic guitar and Alex Kuz's saz play. Overall I like this one pretty well. (9.125/10)3. "Joreil" (5:30) Alexander's use of saz as the lead instrument in this is welcome: creating a very inviting, very warm melody within the thick featherbed weave of heavily-distorted and -chorused gentle electric guitar strumming, driving bass and drums and, soon, accordion. Switching to volume-pedal controlled electric lead guitar, Alexander continues some excellent melodic soloing with Arkady Fedotov's acoustic guitar and Alexander Koryukovets' accordion also playing some nice "secondary" melody lines within the rich weave. A very pleasant, pleasing sometimes Greek folk-feeling song. (9/10)4. "Tio" (7:11) thought Alexander Kuzovlev's staccato lead guitar line provides the lead, I find Arkady Fedotov's bass play the most enjoyable and interesting thread of this song's first motif. In the early third minute the band switches into a new, smoother and more spacious motif as Ivan leads the way with brother Arkady providing the propellant for Alexander Kuzovlev's new approach to his Jeff Beck "Nadia"-like synthesized guitar lead. At the end of the fifth minute the band switches again onto a more forceful, Math Rock weave for a motif that has them traveling at a breakneck speed as Alexander shreds for a bit before settling into a mathematical melody pattern (even doubling it up with a second lead STEVE VAI-like electric guitar line) taking the song to its conclusion. Nice song! (13.5/15)5. "Akcani" (5:47) a song that is infused with a Russian folk feel not unlike Uzbekestan prog band FROM.UZ's earlier material. I like the use of unorthodox drum and percussion sounds as well as the doubling up of Alexander's main melody line by Arkady and, sometimes, Vladimir and Alexander Korykovets' accordion. The prominent use of the saz in the second half only solidifies the "Eastern" feelings oozing from this song (which I like). (8.875/10)6. "Plake" (6:53) the sound palette of this one has, for me, an almost-Caribbean flavor--like something one might have heard from world music artists Strunz & Farah or Govi back in the 80s or 90s but the hyper-speed pace provided by Ivan is much different than those artists, and then come the Kosmisches space synthesizer and mandoline sounds mixed into the weave. This is followed by another section with Alexander Kuz playing his volume-pedaled lead guitar followed by more straightforward axe playing for a bit before reverting to the "new" volume-pedal-controlled note playing. I like the world music feel of the first half but have to admit that this is one of those songs on which Ivan Fedotov's drumming just feels incongruous and unfit. (13.25/15)7. "Capitli" (4:30) a cool guitar weave, acoustic and electric, with great bass and accordion worked into the weave quite thickly while Ivan provides a wave-like rhythm track beneath it all. Alex Kuz enters in the middle with his lead electric, culminating in a bridge of staccato-chord pulses punctuation to transition us back into the gentler domain akin to the opening. Arkady's fretless lines here are great--matching perfectly Alex's volume-pedal-controled lead noteplay. I like this one very much. (9.125/10)8. "Far" (6:24) opening with more of Alex Kuzovlev's new Steve Vai/Jeff Beck-borrowed volume-pedal-controlled "centerless" note play, the band soon joins in providing another unusual world music (Caribbean/Yacht Rock) foundational weave for Alex to microtonally bend his notes over. The chorus "B" section finds the band traveling into some jazzier, almost heavy metal pathways while Alex continues his explorations of Steve Vai territory. The fourth minute is quite askew, feeling like a modern rock/metallized take on some of Dick Dale's 1960s Surfer Rock. Interesting! Never boring and, to be honest, not bad! (9/10)Total Time 48:30While I like the band's use of more regionally-traditional instruments (saz, mandoline, acoustic guitar, accordion) and the "world music" feels generated by such choices and combinations, I'm not as much of a fan of Alexander Kuzovlev's melody or sound choices. The Steve Vai/Jeff Beck like guitar tone/sound that he's now obsessed with is interesting but, in my opinion, is only a gimmick that should be used sparingly so that it doesn't get old or overwhelming, not on every song. As is not unusual, Ivan Fedotov's drumming, in my opinion, is occasionally unbefitting the music or weave: as if his sense of rhythm is different, even in conflict with, the rest of the band. The best and most consistently pleasing elements of this album's music, for me, are Arkady Fedotov's exquisite bass play and the enriching qualities of Alexander Koryukovets's accordion and Vladimir Ryabinin's comforting acoustic guitar tracks. Obviously, this album, for me, in no way reaches the heights of near-perfection that their 2023 masterpiece De ludo globi did. Still, this is another quite fine album: by no means a dud. B+/4.5 stars; another great collection of songs from these excellent musicians and unique craftsmen--once again defying categorization due to their idiosyncratic blending of diverse and eclectic styles and sounds. While not a masterpiece, this is not an album to be trifled with. Highly recommended.
items._genre: psychedelic rock / space rock / world fusion / folk rock
items._cn_summary: 俄罗斯乐队VESPERO的第17张录音室专辑延续了其迷幻与太空摇滚的核心方向，同时大量融入俄罗斯民间音乐元素。手风琴、萨兹琴等传统乐器与电吉他、无品贝斯、失真合成器交织，形成跨文化对话。多首作品采用多主题并置结构，在爵士摇滚、民谣旋律与迷幻音景之间自由切换，编曲层次丰富。评论者特别提到双主音吉他线条的运用、贝斯手Arkady Fedotov的无品贝斯表现，以及手风琴与电声乐器之间的色彩对比。部分曲目在编曲上略显松散，鼓手与乐队偶有脱节，但整体氛围温暖且具探索性。专辑体现了东欧乐队在长期创作中保持进化能力的特点，融合手法成熟但实验性有限。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The stars aligned when Supersister recorded their second album; even the aura of their Focus bandmates was present, the ancestral European past alongside avant-garde modernity and free jazz. To the Highest Bidder demonstrated compositional growth, the same compositional rebelliousness, the feeling of transcending genres, but in a different category. A Girl Named You sounds with that same compositional freedom reminiscent of Frank Zappa's 1969 improvisations, and even Eric Dolphy.Taking the time to let the notes float...like leaves on the sea that the wind gathers...and with the freshness of early Jethro Tull, the darkness of late Doors...the sophistication of Jacques Loussier playing Bach in a jazz key...plus the wisdom of the very end of Pawn Hearts by Van Der Graaf Generator.No Tree Will Grow (On Too High a Mountain) begins like those Gong mantras...but a melody sung with such sensitivity that it transcends genre, making it immortal. And in that contrast of warmth and coldness...of wide and intimate spaces, Supersister finds its place, the right note, its star in the firmament.From grandiose arrangements to thin, minimalist notes, with barely any percussion, stripped down like a winter city in Energy (Out of Future). When the otherworldly keyboard and the already prominent drums draw us into a vast courtyard, revealing it piece by piece until we reach the upper floor and gain a comprehensive, all-encompassing vision, exemplified by the music when the organ joins in, bringing light and air.Robert Jan Stips' keyboards alone can convey the essence of Canterbury without needing to travel to Great Britain, because they reside in the mind and heart.With great skill, they could abandon classical arrangements... only to let them fall to the ground and then raise them up in a psychedelic way, mutating and playing along until they arrived at Higher, once again flirting with Bossa Nova and that sweetness of the 60s, the flute, and melodies that, unknowingly, would influence alternative bands of the early 2000s like The Beta Band.The most peripheral of the Canterbury bandmates would be one of the most psychedelically jazzy, without losing the harmony... always ahead of the curve in terms of technology.
items._genre: Canterbury Scene / progressive rock / jazz fusion / psychedelic
items._cn_summary: Supersister第二张专辑展现了坎特伯雷场景中独特的实验精神，将欧洲古典传统与前卫现代性、自由爵士融为一体。Robert Jan Stips的键盘演奏是专辑核心，既能呈现简约到近乎空灵的质感，也能在宏大编曲中构建层次丰富的音景。专辑在多种风格间自由穿梭：既有类似Frank Zappa的即兴自由和Eric Dolphy式的爵士探索，也有Gong式的冥想氛围和早期Jethro Tull的清新感。作品在温暖与冷峻、宏大与私密之间不断转换，部分段落融入Bossa Nova的甜美元素与六十年代旋律感，长笛与键盘的对话贯穿始终。整体呈现出一种超越类型界限的作曲自由，既根植于爵士与古典传统，又充满迷幻色彩和前卫实验意识。

items.excerpt: Review by kev rowland — Can it really be more than 25 years since Lost World released their debut 'Trajectories'? I raved over them (I think it is the only time I have heard a prog band where three of the players were from the Moscow Conservatory) and since then I have kept in touch with Andy Didorenko (acoustic & electric guitars, bass, violins, percussion, keyboard, backing vocals), although it was only after he asked me to review the recent reissues that we realised I had not heard thei
items.body: Review by kev rowland — Can it really be more than 25 years since Lost World released their debut 'Trajectories'? I raved over them (I think it is the only time I have heard a prog band where three of the players were from the Moscow Conservatory) and since then I have kept in touch with Andy Didorenko (acoustic & electric guitars, bass, violins, percussion, keyboard, backing vocals), although it was only after he asked me to review the recent reissues that we realised I had not heard their 2024 album which is why I am playing it now. For the majority of their career LWB have been a band, but this is better regarded as a solo project as while there are three drummers on different tracks, the only other musicians are Yulia Musayelyan (flute on one) and singer Phoebe Carter who is on three. In January 2022 Andy was full of creative energy and by the end of the month he had recorded four demos, but then Russia invaded Ukraine and nothing seemed to matter anymore. Fast forward a year and Andy remembered an anti-war song he had written with Vassilli some 30 years earlier, and resurrected this and another from the same period, provided different lyrics and the album started coming together.Right from the beginning of "Overture 2024" one knows this is going to be something different as the chaotic and over the top piano, bass and violins drive us headlong into "Crumble Down" and it is already obvious that this is not an album where Andy wants us to relax, but rather it is full of jagged edges so we are careful where we step. This is his musical reaction to what was taking place in Ukraine, ensuring that the listener knows it is intended not to be comfortable, and in many ways feels much like a modern classical piece of work than something which is obviously progressive rock. It is dynamic, full of contrast, and even the vocals provide contrast in that they are highly melodic when they appear, very different to the staccato elements, and with a multi-instrumentalist as happy on piano, guitar or violin, one also never knows what melodic lead is going to be next.Even the cover photograph is symbolic, as it was taken on Governors Island, which used to be a 172-acre military base but is now a public park. If only we could turn all military bases back to public land the world would be a much better place, but musically this album knows that is never going to be the case so instead keeps driving us along and making us uncomfortable. This is yet another great album from Andy, I wonder what he is going to come up with next?
items._genre: crossover prog / modern classical / art rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是吉他手兼多乐器演奏家Andy Didorenko在2022年俄乌战争爆发后的个人音乐回应。起初的四首demo在战争开始后被迫中断，直到他重拾三十年前与Vassilli合写的反战歌曲并重新填词，整张专辑才逐渐成形。作品以钢琴、贝斯和小提琴开场，节奏凌厉、棱角分明，拒绝让听众放松舒适，更接近现代古典的质感而非传统前卫摇滚。多乐器演奏者身份使旋律主线不断在钢琴、吉他与小提琴之间切换，人声在出现时极具旋律性，与断续的器乐段落形成鲜明对比。唱片封面取自曾为军事基地的Governors Island，象征着将军事用地归还民用的理想，整体概念与音乐情绪紧密咬合。虽以solo project形式呈现，但仍邀请了三位鼓手、长笛及客座人声参与录制，层次丰富。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 新专辑延续其模糊边界的创作风格，将民谣、前卫音乐与宗教氛围融合为一体。演奏以中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴和钢琴为核心，并加入鼓、贝斯和合成器拓宽音色层次。多数曲目为即兴创作，一遍录音完成，呈现出一种穿越时空的静谧神秘感。专辑核心曲目《Sprigs of Heather》以中世纪圣乐式的开场引入，缓缓流淌的钢琴旋律成为全作最精致的段落。整张作品是 Cotton 献给 2024 年底去世父亲的纪念专辑，曲目中弥漫着深切的哀思与温柔的怀旧，光与暗在不同乐章间交替流动，难以被归入单一类型。音乐既向听众发出挑战，也带来情感上的满足。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._genre: world music / African fusion / Puxa / dance
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了圣多美和普林西比1970至80年代的Puxa音乐，展示了这一非洲葡语国家在所谓黄金时代的声音遗产。Puxa融合了来自其他葡语非洲殖民地的元素，并掺入merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等节奏，据称具有召灵驱魔的功能。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队在《Sossegado》中呈现闷声吉他即兴与鼓手的对峙，Sangazuza在贝斯和键盘退出后让鼓与吉他撑起律动。十五首曲目中多重吉他交织缠绕，主唱与和声彼此呼应，延伸出可让舞者沉浸数小时的绵长律动。Africa Negra的曲目是这种漂浮感吉他的典型例证。整张合辑呈现出小岛屿音乐场景在有限录音条件下依然迸发的丰富创造力。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威乐手组成三重奏，演绎斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材，但刻意跳出舞蹈伴奏功能，转向室内乐式的亲密对话。三位演奏者均有跨界经历：长笛/萨克斯手曾在挪威先锋融合乐队中活动，打击乐手活跃于多个模糊流派界限的项目中。评论指出专辑开篇选用挪威塞特斯达尔山谷的「瀑布精灵」传说曲，暗示传统民间舞曲表层欢快之下暗藏的不安底色，这种对民间音乐深层意涵的挖掘贯穿整张唱片。编曲中旋律线条时有分解、节奏停顿，器乐间留有大量即兴呼吸空间，传统素材被解构后重新拼贴，形成介于民俗音乐、前卫即兴与现代室内乐之间的独特声响。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa的专辑《Sendas》（Pathways）诞生于2021年疫情封锁期间，在意大利Fazioli钢琴厂的音乐厅完成录制。整张专辑源自两小时无脚本的独奏即兴录音，后期混入稀疏的人声采样、打击乐、循环、野外录音和拾得音效。Sosa本人拒绝被归类为爵士、拉丁或古典，强调"没有错误的音符"，崇尚"少即是多"的美学。他关注人类精神层面的迷失，期望音乐能引发深层共鸣。专辑第一轨《Inside the Spirit》以对钢琴弦的拨弄与抚摸开场，缓慢展开对乐器共鸣内核的探索。整张作品体现了即兴创作中沉思与不安分的创造力结合。
